runs.analysis:
Both candidates follow the schema (omissions and potential_improvements, each item with issue, explanation and recommendation). Both ground their points in the project context: the 50-100 MW energy gap, cyber risk to surveillance systems, Strait of Gibraltar traffic, legal complexity, stakeholder engagement and innovation.

Candidate A is concise and has 6 omissions and 6 improvements. Its distinctive catches are decommissioning ownership and the lack of a Chief Engineer or technical authority. It also covers climate adaptation and integration of structural and geotechnical monitoring. It misses several important gaps: supply chain and logistics (a Critical strategic lever in the plan), dedicated risk and insurance management, QA and validation gate ownership, and occupational medicine for a workforce of 8,000-12,000 on offshore platforms. It also contains a small internal inconsistency, saying "eight distinct directors" and then listing five.

Candidate B has 9 omissions and 9 improvements. It covers the same core gaps as A (energy, cyber, maritime, legal, communications, R&D) and adds supply chain, risk management and insurance, QA and validation, and occupational health and diving medicine. These are real, plan-relevant gaps. Its improvements are also decision-useful. They cover decision rights and escalation, contractor versus full-time continuity (based on the min/max staffing in the team data), ownership of the Environmental Oversight Board, KPIs, the pre-construction to operations baseline handoff, governance of the neutral consortium, succession and knowledge management, and the org chart. Its weaknesses are heavy verbosity and some role bloat, since it proposes many new directors on top of an existing team of about 8. It also misses decommissioning. Even so, it is more thorough and shows closer reading of the team document and the risk register.

Overall B is more complete and more useful downstream. A is tighter but leaves out several significant omissions.

Both candidates identify real gaps tied to the plan: energy infrastructure, cybersecurity, maritime traffic in the Strait, legal, and stakeholder engagement. Both also catch the missing energy plan flagged in the pre-project assessment.

Candidate A is very thorough but bloated. It proposes nine new director-level roles on top of an existing team of about eight. These include Supply Chain, Risk, QA, R&D, Occupational Medicine and others. It does not weigh this against the team's size or the budget, and it never prioritizes among them. Several of its omissions overlap with existing roles or are weakly justified. The occupational medicine item, for example, stretches the plan: the tunnel is a pressurized rail corridor, not a saturation-diving operation. Its improvements are long and partly generic: KPIs, succession planning, an org chart, stakeholder management. The stakeholder item largely duplicates the Communications omission. Some of its recommendations are invented specifics, such as compensation links, approval thresholds in euros, and named firms. It also has a small naming inconsistency, "Environmental Compliance Director".

Candidate B is more concise and better prioritized. It has six omissions, all anchored in the plan. Decommissioning is a distinctive and valid catch, since a 20-year project with a €2-4B reserve has no owner for the end-of-life plan. Its improvements are specific and insightful. They cover the missing Chief Engineer or technical authority, integration of structural and geotechnical monitoring, a digital twin and data infrastructure, climate adaptation ownership, and consortium-versus-government escalation. It makes one small error, calling the 20-year project a "20-year operational lifespan". Its recommendations are less detailed, but they are actionable and avoid over-expanding the team.

Overall, B is more decision-useful and better calibrated. A is more exhaustive but verbose, repetitive and over-prescriptive.

A is concise and plan-specific (Decision 2, the 75% local hiring target, the 128.8 km² holding cost, FX variance) but misses key gaps: no physical security/resilience owner and no tenant acquisition owner, even though tenant commitments gate expansion. It also mislabels ARS as the water-rights authority, and some improvements are process add-ons rather than team fixes. B covers the more consequential gaps: environmental/water lead, EPC program manager, tenant/revenue lead, security architect, plus governance, the FTE-vs-IC assignment for Grid & Power, and succession. It ties them to plan specifics (Risk 9 remediation overrun, 60% take-or-pay gate, DREAL). B has some generic padding (digital twin, advisory board, overlapping controls roles), and its workforce-manager omission may partly duplicate an existing role. Overall B is more useful for downstream planning.

Candidate A names the gaps that matter most for this plan: environmental and water lead, EPC/construction manager, tenant acquisition lead, physical security and resilience architect, and workforce delivery. These tie directly to the prompt's gating items (tenant take-or-pay, DREAL/EIA, brownfield remediation, sabotage resilience, local hiring). It cites plan-specific details such as Decision 4's 60% threshold, Risk 9's remediation overrun and the FTE/IC split. Its weaknesses are bloat and some generic padding. Examples are the digital twin manager, succession planning, advisory board and a separate project controls role that overlaps the EPC manager. The workforce omission may also overlap an existing "Local Workforce Orchestrator" role, which B mentions.

Candidate B is tighter and more clever in places. It uses the €4.32B FX variance and the 128.8 km² buffer holding cost. It also proposes useful mechanisms: RFP scoring weights for local hiring, a gate sign-off report, and a security steering committee. But it has fewer omissions and misses tenant strategy ownership and a dedicated security architect, both core to the prompt. Some recommendations are odd: it assigns QA/QC to the Strategist, and the ARS-versus-DREAL water claim is shaky. It also treats water risk as a single medium-risk item without an environmental lead.

Overall, A's coverage of the real structural team gaps is better for downstream use, despite its padding. B is sharper but less complete.

Candidate A is more substantive and decision-useful. Its omissions are real gaps tied to the plan. No role owns the public reference distributor, which is a €150M budget item. No role runs the €900M capacity-building and grant program. There is also no national-regulator relations function, no data-quality governance, and no financial operations or billing owner. It cites specific decisions, risks and deadlines. Its improvements are also practical: a RACI matrix, a committee structure, a check of the 35-FTE requirement against the visible team, audit ownership, and an owner for each contingency action. Weaknesses: it is verbose and recommends many new roles, which could bloat the team. It also wrongly lists BEUC as a disability advocacy group. Some improvements overlap.

Candidate B is shorter and more cautious. Several of its points are low-value, such as a logistics assistant for the testing team and a test-wave handoff protocol. Its omissions are narrower. Its suggestion to fold public grant administration into the Financial Specialist's role adds more load to a role that is already stretched. It does flag the accessibility-standards coordination gap and the IT cost audit need, which are useful. Overall it gives less coverage of the major structural gaps.

Candidate B finds the larger structural gaps in the team. It notes that no role owns the €900M capacity-building and grant programme. It notes that no one leads the public reference distributor (Decision 11, €150M). It also notes that national regulators have no dedicated liaison, which matters because enforcement depends on them. It adds roles for stakeholder communications, data-quality governance, accessibility design and billing operations. Its improvements are useful for downstream stages: a RACI matrix, committee authority, testing-versus-standards escalation, and a reconciliation of the stated 35 FTE against the visible roster. It also ties actions to the pre-project-assessment deadlines. Weaknesses: it is very long, it recommends many new roles (possible bloat), and it has small slips, such as calling BEUC a disability body and citing a "15% testing FTE" figure that may not exist. Candidate A is concise and references the plan's decisions and risks, but its omissions are mostly minor: a logistics assistant, a standards-maintenance engineer, and an IT auditor. It misses the large gaps, namely capacity building, the reference distributor and national regulators. Several of its improvements are thin or just reshuffle existing responsibilities. Overall B is more insightful and more useful, despite its verbosity.

Candidate A is thorough and plan-specific. It cites the Month 4 gate KPIs, the €300k contingency, the Leipzig-Grünau outreach base, Review Issues 2 and 3, and Risks 3, 7 and 8. It finds real gaps: no finance owner for the €1.5M release, no real-time KPI monitoring, no volunteer coordination, no succession plan for the single-threaded Incident Commander, and no field-safety incident function. Its weaknesses are role bloat (about seven new roles for an eight-person team, which clashes with the prompt's staffing-realism constraint and ignores cost), some generic boilerplate (org chart, RACI, scorecards), and overlap between items. Candidate B is concise and realistic: a part-time admin to track the budget tranches, a QA sample of installations, volunteer overnight cover, and shifting the Contract Manager to SLA enforcement after Month 2. It is thin. It misses succession, real-time monitoring, and governance authority gaps. It uses placeholder-like references ("Decision X"). One recommendation, having the Incident Commander personally approve all misinformation statements, creates a bottleneck. Overall A is more insightful and more useful downstream despite the bloat.

Candidate A gives 3 omissions and 3 improvements. Some are plan-aware (finance tracking, QA sampling of home kits, overnight surge coverage), but it leaves a "Decision X" placeholder and recommends that the Incident Commander personally approve all counter-misinformation statements, which would bottleneck a crisis. Its quarterly script review is low-value, and it misses real-time KPI monitoring ahead of the M4 gate, facility operations, volunteer management, and single points of failure. Candidate B gives 6 omissions and 8 improvements, mostly tied to plan specifics: the €3.5M staged budget and €300k contingency, the M4 gate KPIs, Leipzig-Grünau, German Barrierefreiheit, and numbered risks. It finds real gaps (no real-time KPI monitoring before the gate, no facility operations or accessibility owner, no volunteer coordination despite volunteer safety being a named risk, no backup for single-person FTE roles). Its authority matrix and data feedback loop are useful. Weaknesses are that it proposes many new roles, which strains the limited-staffing and budget constraints, and that some items (org chart, RACI, scorecards) are generic padding. Overall B is more thorough, specific and useful downstream.
